Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 118, to amend the Government Railways Act.
Explain.

This is to put the Government railways under the railway commission, just the same as any other railways, with the exception of claims against the railway and the expropriation clauses of the Railway Act.
The minister's statement is rather indefinite. Does that mean that the operation of the Government railways will be placed under the board, or simply the freight and passenger tariffs?
It includes everything except expropriation clauses and claims against the Government railways
The railways will be operated by the Government?
Oh, yes.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On the Orders of the Day:

I desire to ask the Government or the Minister of Militia for information regarding the publication of the answer of Colonel Bruce to the so-called Babtie report. I should also like to know whether the Babtie who is at the head of the commission inquiring into Dr. Bruce's report is the same Dr. Babtie who was involved in the notorious scandal in connection with the British Medical Service in Mesopotamia, and who has been practically relegated from the service.

I speak subject to correction, but I think the last time this question was asked in the House the Prime Minister stated that he proposed sending Dr.
244*
Bruce's report to the minister of the overseas forces for consideration, 'before laying it on the Table, and he gave certain reasons for that. I know nothing more about the matter than what was stated by the Prime Minister at the time. With regard to my hon. friend's other question about General Babtie, I have heard nothing about the matter to which he refers.
Sir SAM HUG-HES: Surely the Government would not let a valuable document like that pass out of their hands without keeping a copy. I might say that it would be possible for me to furnish the Government with a copy if they have not got one. I think in the interests of the country the report .should be laid on the Table and printed for distribution.

I will draw the
Prime Minister's attention to the matter.
Is the report of Dr. Bruce being witheld until some answer to it can be prepared?

I have no more
information on the subject than was given to the House by the Prime Minister, but I shall be glad to direct his attention to my hon. friend's question.

As this matter comes under the Militia Department, and as there is no Minister of Militia except my hon. friend and the so-called acting minister in England, how is it that my hon. friend comes to this Parliament and says, as Minister of Militia, that he knows nothing whatever about this matter? If he does not know, who does? Why has not Dr. Bruce's report been laid on the Table?

The Prime Minister gave what I presume was a satisfactory answer to the House a short time ago, since then no further information on the subject has come before me. The matter was one which the minister of the overseas forces has to do. He is a colleague of mine, in control of the overseas forces in Great Britain. He is subject to the Prime Minister's direction, and not to that of the Minister of Militia, as my hon. friend seems to think.
Are we to understand that there are two Ministers of Militia, one here -and one on the other side, although there is no constitutional authority for the appointment of that other one?

The order in council creating the position of minister of over-

seas forces was laid on the Table. It states exactly what his position is and what his duties are. He reports to the Prime Minister.
On the Orders of the Day:

Mr. Speaker, when the vote was taken on the third reading of Bill No. 75, Military Service Act, 1917, I was not in my seat in the House. I was under the impression that the vote would be only taken during the night, so that I was aboard the train on my way to Ottawa -when the vote was taken. I wish to state that, if I had been here, I would have registered my vote against the measure.

Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY St. John City):	I should like to ask a question of
the Minister of Militia-

Which one?
iSir EDWfARD KEMP:	I am the one
here.

We have two Ministers of Militia, and it is sometimes rather confusing. The question I wish to ask is of very great importance as affecting recruiting, if the opportunity for voluntary enlistment has not been entirely cut off. I am informed that the Veterans' Association in the city of St. John, composed of nearly 300 returned soldiers, has recently passed a very strong resolution protesting against the employment in New Brunswick of men and officers-and some of the officers are employed at very high salaries- who have not been to the front. The opinion expressed by the veterans is that these positions ought to be given to men and officers who have been to the front. I understand that a copy of the resolution has been forwarded to my hon. friend the Minister of Miutia. I would like to- ask him if he has received the resolution, and what 'action he purposes taking with regard to it.

The resolution to which my hon. friend refers has not yet reached me. There is a good deal to be said in respect of the opinion expressed by the

Veteran's Association, as set out by my hon. friend from St. John. There are a certain number of surplus officers in Canada, and we are having the matter investigated by a competent board, with a view to seeing which officers should be retained, and which can be dispensed with, so that they may revert to civil life, particularly at this time when there are better opportunities for employment than there may be when the war closes. The matter is actually under investigation.
On the Orders of the Day:

When the estimates of the Minister of Inland Revenue were under discussion last night, the minister promised that a list of the temporary preventive officers of his department would be placed on Hansard. This list does not appear in Hansard. I do not think that is treating the IjTousa fairly. The estimates were passed with the understanding that this list would be furnished, and I ask that it be placed on Hansard tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue is not present at the moment, but I may say that a member of the Hansard staff spoke to me last night when I was leaving the Chamber, and stated it would be irregular to place such a list upon Hansard unless it had been read in the House.
Except by consent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is probably the explanation of the fact that the statement does not appear in Hansard. However, I shall bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Inland Revenue.

The Minister of Inland Revenue was quite ready to read the list last night, and it was only by unanimous consent of the committee that its reading was dispensed with, with the understanding that it would he given to Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will direct the attention of the minister to the point. Hansard, of course, would have no objection of embodying such a list in the report, if it is regular to do so. I should think it could be done with the unanimous consent of the House, but not otherwise. I assume the House is unanimous in consenting to it.
And consent being given.

House in committee on Bill No. 53, an Act respecting insurance.-Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Since this Bill
was betore the House it has been carefully considered toy the Banking and Commerce Committee. I explained upon its introduction that I was extremely reluctant to take up so important, and so extensive a measure of legislation at this session of the House, but that the insurance business was, by reason of a decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council which challenged the constitutionality of the Dominion Insurance Act, in such a condition that this legislation is deemed absolutely necessary in order that the Department of Insurance may exercise proper control over that business throughout the Dominion.
On section 3-Application of Act:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Bill with the amendments made by the Banking and

$94,250 00	$94,250 00
Commerce Committee has not been reprinted. The Banking and Commerce Committee made an amendment to subsection 2 of section 3 of the Bill, as follows:
(2a) To any contract entered into or any certificate of membership or policy of insurance issued before the twentieth day of July, eighteen hundred and eighty-five by any assessment life insurance company.
This is sim.ply a transfer of an existing section 75 from another part of the Act to this section, where it would appear to be more appropriately placed.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Licenses:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have an amendment to subsection 3 of section 4-[DOT]
Was section 3 passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, but we
would be glad to consider anything my hon. friend may have to suggest.

Section 3 refers to the application of the Act, and states the cases to which it shall not apply. For instance:

To any contract of marine or inland marine insurance effected in Canada by any company authorized to carry on within Canada the said business.
What was the reason of this exception? If the Act applies to all Canada, why does it not apply to a contract of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The reason is that it is not possible for any one country to control marine insurance, which may be effected anywhere. That is the explanation given me by the Superintendent of Insurance. I have not a personal knowledge of it myself, any more than my right hon. friend has, but it seems to me a reasonable explanation.

I would hardly think because a contract of marine insurance is universal, it applies to all countries. Neither this country nor any other country can have any legislative control over it. If you make a contract of insurance in London, or Paris, or any other part of the world, it must be subject to the law of some country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The superintendent informs me that the risk is upon the high seas and consequently it is not possible, in his opinion, for the Government of any country to effectually control marine insurance.

That would apply to
marine insurance on the high seas but the Bill also excepts inland marine insurance, which would cover insurance on the great lakes and on rivers and insurance in the different provinces, which would be entirely within the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada. My hon. friend must get a better reason than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The reason I have given is a very good one. The exception applies to ocean marine insurance as well as inland marine insurance. I was addressing myself first to the question of marine insurance, that is to the question of marine insurance, and the answer which the Superintendent of Insurance gives seems to me to be a very reasonable one. At all events, 1 believe his opinion is entitled to weight in the matter. As far as inland marine insurance companies are concerned, I am informed that a change was made in 1910, when my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was Prime Minister. It was made by reason of representations, which would seem to me to be well founded, that it would not be fair to subject the agents of inland marine insurance companies to the
provisions of this Act in competition as they are for business with companies not subject to the jurisdiction of the Dominion of Canada. I can understand that there is a real difference between marine insurance and other kinds of insurance as far as this Parliament is concerned. At all events I would point out to my hon. friend that if there is any objection to it there was the same objection to it in 1910 when my right hon. friend made an exception of this kind of insurance.

If my hon.
friend would always be as careful to respect the laws passed by the former regime it would be all the better for him. In the meantime, I am not satisfied with the reason given us why, as a general proposition, we cannot legislate on this question, because of the universal form of the contract, applying as it does to the high seas. I am satisfied that they have a law in Great Britain on the matter. If my memory serves me aright, in my time we had some correspondence with the British authorities on the subject. They claimed that they could legislate on these matters as against the colonies. For the reason that their shipping is much more important than ours, they claimed jurisdiction. We did not always agree with them but still we did not contest the point. There must be some law somewhere and if they can legislate on the subject, why can 'we not legislate here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think there is no doubt that we can legislate, that we - have the power to legislate, but it is not regarded as expedient that we should legislate upon this question because the companies subject to our legislation would be in competition with companies outside and they would not get the insurance business.

Does not that argument lose force when you come to consider that there is the same competition in regard to fire insurance? One of the greatest competitors of the fire insurance companies established in Canada arises from the operations of the mutual companies of the United States. They insure properties in Canada, and although they have never made a deposit with the Government, they do a very large business. It is true that the contract cannot be enforced in Canada. A party sustaining a loss caused by the destruction of, or damage to, his property cannot recover against these mutual companies in Canada but must go to the country in which they are located for the pur-

pose of enforcing his rights. They are very large competitors of the legalized insurance companies having their offices in Canada. The same argument, in so far as fire insurance is concerned, would apply to the case of marine insurance. As my right hon. friend has stated, marine insurance companies are incorporated in Canada. Some companies are incorporated in Canada and other companies are licensed to do business in Canada. I do not see why the law should not he made to apply to marine insurance companies just as well as to fire and life insurance companies. The Minister of Finance has stated that some years ago, under certain legislation, marine insurance companies were excepted. I understand the object of the present law is to get over difficulties in regard to insurance which have arisen by reason of the decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The minister apparently is urging the passage of this Bill, which is of enormous importance at the- present time, because of an intimation that decisions of the Privy Council have thrown the insurance business into a state of confusion. If they have it seems to me that their judgment would affect the position of marine insurance companies. If it is desirable to pass a general Act which would relieve the insurance companies from the difficulties caused by the decisions of the court, I think it ought to be applied to all insurance companies doing business in Canada as well as to fire and life insurance companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No question has been raised as to this exception which was inserted in the Act. The case is not at all on all fours with that of the fire insurance companies which are licensed to do business here, which have to conform to the conditions of this Act and which are in competition with the mutuals outside of Canada. There are no marine insurance companies complaining of this legislation. In 1910, I find representations were made by the transportation companies that unless these companies were exempted from the provisions of this Insurance Act there would be discrimination against the St. Lawrence route and Canadian ports generally in so far as insurance was concerned, which would mean an increase in insurance rates and an increase in freight rates upon the St. Lawrence route. If my hon. friend desires that these inland marine insurance companies should be subjected to the provisions of this Act, and if we should meet his request, it would only mean that ocean freight rates to his own port of St.

John and on the St. Lawrence route would be injuriously affected. My hon. friend does not want to bring that about. It seems to me that his objection is ill founded.
, It is true that we are bringing this measure down by reason of the decision of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council raised no objection to inland marine insurance companies being exempted from the privisions of this Act, nor did they advert to the status of these companies in their decision. By reason of that decision, because it is so far reaching, it is unfortunately necessary that we should re-enact the entire Insurance Bill, and that is why we are now considering this section with all the other sections, although it was not touched by the decision of the law lords of the Privy Council.

X .spent a good deal of time in the committee when the Insurance Act was enacted in 1910, and the reason given by the minister is the reason why we exempted these marine insurance companies. Besides that, there has since been no trouble over it, so far as I know. I do [DOT]a good deal of marine insurance when I am at home, and I have never experienced any difficulty since that time.
By what law is it regulated, the British Act?

The British Act. So far *as concerns any companies doing business in Canada that I know of, they are regulated by the British Act, and we have not interfered with them. We did not interfere with them then because it was represented to us that this might make a difference to the St. Lawrence route insurance, and also to the inland waters insurance. That is why we exempted -this marine insurance at that time, and this Bill makes no change from the Act of 1910.
On section 4-Licenses may be granted to Canadian and foreign companies:

In -section 4 there is a claus-e providing for Lloyd's Association to be licensed to do. bu-si-ness in Canada. Would that include the right to carry on -marine insurance? Provision is -m-ade in -section 3 that such an association may be licensed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Permissive:
-Mr. SINCLAIR:	That wo-uld mean that
they can carry on marine insurance in -Canada if licensed?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They may apply for ,a license, but they would not do so because they are exempt undeT section 3, which we have been discussing. It is open to a marine insurance company to take out a license under the Act, but as that entails a certain deposit and a fulfilment of the requirements of the Act, it is not at all probable that any marine company would take out a license, as they are exempted from doing so under section 3.

Subsection 2 of this section provides that a foreign company incorporated outside Canada, the moment it becomes licensed to do business in Canada, shall be deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada; in other words, shall be deemed to be a company incorporated under the Canadian company law.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

Why not? How on earth can it be deemed to be a company if incorporated under the laws of Canada unless it is deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws which provide for the incorporation of Canadian companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I quite appreciate the point raised. It attracted my own attention, and it has been carefully considered by the Deputy Minister of Justice. If my hon. friend will turn to the interpretation section and look at the definition of " Canadian company" he will find that that definition excludes any British or foreign company " which becomes incorporated under the provisions of this Act by reason merely of obtaining a license from the minister .as herein .authorized." That, therefore, excludes from the meaning of the words " Canadian company " any British or foreign company which becomes incorporated under the provisions of this Act by reason of obtaining a license under the Act.
To come back to subsection 1, which is under immediate consideration, my hon. friend's point is, will the effect of this legislation be to make, let us say, a New York incorporation a Canadian corporation? I need not say to my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley), as .a good lawyer, that it is not within the power of this Parliament to make a New York corporation into a Canadian corporation.
You attempt to do if.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I .am sound in my law as to that. In .the first place, the Dominion Government has not jurisdiction to
do it. There is nothing clearer than this: that a company incorporated under the laws of any country remains subject to the laws of that country; that is to say, its domicile is that country. It is open to this Parliament to say that a foreign company shall be deemed to be a (Canadian company for the purposes of this Act, but that does not make it a Canadian company in the same *sense 'as a Canadian company incorporated under .the Dominion Companies Act.

The minister does not limit it to the word "deemed;" it says it shall thereupon .and thereby become and be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada; not merely " deemed to be," but " shall be."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then let us say still I .am correct, because, in the first place, this Parliament, no matter what words are *used, cannot make .a New York insurance company into ia Canadian corporation. That is the .starting point.
Then why attempt to do it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because, for the purposes of this Act, it is necessary to put it in precisely the same position as a Canadian company. I made a suggestion myself, which the Deputy Minister of Justice ruled against, that it should be made clear that, by the insertion of the words "for the purposes of this Act," we were not trying to make a foreign corporation a Dominion corporation. The Deputy Minister of Justice, however, upon a full consideration of the purposes and effect of the Bill, by this section confirmed these words that my hon. friend now takes exception to, and did not regard it as expedient that the words "for the purposes of this Act" should be inserted after the word "be." All I can say to my hon. friend is that we are trying now to make the Act constitutional. The constitutionality of the Act has often been impugned, and recently so in a rather vague way, the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has declared it so. In that decision it was suggested that it would be possible for the Dominion Parliament to frame legislation, providing the wording was apt, which would give it the jurisdiction which we now seek to regulate the insurance business in. Canada. These sections which we now have under consideration have received the most painstaking attention on the part of the Deputy Minister of Justice and outside counsel.
What outside counsel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think Christopher Eobinson of Toronto. I hesitate, therefore, to make any change in this wording, which has been so carefully considered and deemed essential, in order that this Act may be held to be constitutional, should its constitutionality be challenged, as it has been in the past.

I have the greatest possible respect for the Deputy Minister of Justice, for his legal standing and great knowledge, and for the ability of Mr. Christopher Eobinson. He is a young man of great ability doubtless, but these men are not legislators here. The responsibility is upon us, the members of this Parliament, and notwithstanding what my hon. friend says as to their opinion, it strikes me as a most anomalous and extraordinary thing to use the language which is contained in this section. There have been	two or	three occasions on
which Parliament has given to foreign companies incorporated outside, the status of companies incorporated in Canada. I remember one occasion when a telegraph company, incorporated in France, I think, was given the status and powers of a company incorporated in Canada. I think a company incorporated in the state of New York was given power toy the New Brunswick legislature to operate a street railway in New Brunswick, when I was a member of the Government of that province, or at all events, a member of the legislature. It was given power to operate in New Brunswick, the same as if it were incorporated in that province. But there are very rare instances where such a power has been given. It has always been the poliey of this Parliament, and the policy of the legislatures, when people seek to get the status of a company to operate in Canada, to tell them to go to the Parliament, or to the legislatures of the provinces, and receive their corporate powers. By this section it is proposed to make a foreign company a corporation under the laws of Canada, not merely for the purpose of this Act, which I might be able to understand, but with this extraordinary section, for which there is no precedent in the legislation of this Parliament, or, I venture to say, in the legislation of any legislature of any province in Canada. I declare most positively there is no precedent for this extraordinary language. It is provided that a foreign company incorporated by a foreign legislature shall, the moment the license is granted, 
become a corporation under the laws of Canada. The section reads:
Any company other than a Canadian company which may obtain from the minister a license or a renewal of a license shall thereupon and thereby become and be deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada with power to carry on throughout Canada, or in such part or parts of Canada as may be specified in the license, the various branches or kinds of insurance which the license may authorize.
Why does the hon. gentleman object to it?
Because it is unnecessary, and if you are going to incorporate a foreign company under the laws of Canada, you must know what powers you are giving to that company.
We give them all the powers a Canadian company would have, as long as they take out a license.
Let us do that, but dc not let us make them a corporate body.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: W)e do not have to.

My hon. friend is wrong when he says: We do not have to. If a company is incorporated in Canada, and becomes a Canadian company, in order to become such, it must be incorporated, either by this Parliament ot under the Companies' Act of Canada. If it is incorporated by Parliament, certain restrictions and limitations are thrown round its incorporation. If it is incorporated under the Companies Act, it becomes liable to all the obligations imposed by the Companies Act. It has the powers which are conferred by the Companies Act, but here we propose, in vague and general terms, to create that foreign company a company under the laws of Canada. Under what laws? Under the Companies Act?	-
Under this law.
No, not under this law.
The moment we license them they become a company.

They become a company under the laws of Canada. Are they under the Companies Act? Will the provisions of the Companies Act apply to them and govern their meetings, if they have meetings in Canada? Will it govern their obligations in Canada? Will the Companies Act apply generally to such a company, so far as applicable? The hon. gentleman will see they are not to become a company merely under this law and for the purposes of this law. If that were so, I could under-

stand it, and I do not know that I would have any objection to it, but they are to become a company under the laws of Canada, and every law which applies to companies in Canada would necessarily apply to these companies which take out licenses. The Minister of Finance says that this is controlled or regulated by paragraph (d) which reads:
"Company" means any corporation incorporated under the laws of Canada or under the laws of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland or of any British possession other than a province of Canada, or of any foreign country for the purpose of carrying on the business of insurance.
That does not affect it at all. That^ simply gives the definition of the word "company." Why could the minister not say that this section applies to any company incorporated in a foreign country, obtaining a license to carry on business in Canada? Why is it necessary to transform a foreign company into a company incorporated under the laws of Canada? Why state a falsehood in the statute? Why put in the statute a provision which is a farce, not a reality? My hon. friend has stated that we cannot make a foreign company a Canadian incorporated company, no matter what language we use. Why, then, use language which cannot effect the contemplated result?
Can we not make a foreign company come under the laws of Canada, so far as Canadian business is concerned?	-
Undoubtedly we can.
That is all we are doing here.	.

We are doing much more than that. We are declaring by section 2 that any foreign company obtaining a license shall thereby become and be deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada, with power to carry on throughout Canada the business of insurance.
What would be the objection to a foreign company becoming a company incorporated under the laws of Canada?	[DOT]

The objection is manifest. The law of Canada governing companies is the Companies Act. There are a hundred provisions of that Act to which a foreign company would not want to be amenable. Is it intended to make all the provisions of the Companies Act applicable
to foreign companies, or is it not? Does my hon. friend (Mr. Middlebro) think that we can do that? Does he think that we intend to do that?
I do not think that we can make a foreign company a Canadian company against its will.
But we are going to do that.
We are not going to do that, because we cannot.
Then if we cannot do it, why attempt to do it?
For the purposes of this Act.

It is not for the purposes of this Act. The minister wanted the words:
" for the purposes of this Act " put in, but the, Deputy Minister of Justice advised against that; therefore the provision is not designed only for the purposes of this Act. Any company which comes under this provision will be deemed an incorporation under the laws of Canada for all purposes. If this section passes, the moment a foreign company obtains a license under this Act, it thereby, under the clear language of the section, becomes a company incorporated under the laws of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To the extent of Dominion jurisdiction only.
If it becomes a company incorporated under the laws of Canada, surely it becomes a Canadian corporation; surely the company laws of Canada then apply to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then what laws of Canada do apply to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This Act.

It does not say this Act. Sir THOMAS WHITE: No other Act.
Mr. PUGSLEY. Then why not say, under this Act? I see no objection to providing that foreign eompanies should become and be deemed to be incorporated for the purposes of this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not, either.

My hon. friend is right in his view, and I think that if he had had his way he would have been doing the sensible thing. If Parliament passes this section in its present form, it will be doing

something unparalleled in legislation., and for which no good reason has been stated.
Sir THOM1AS WHITE: I am very much more modest than my hon. friend. I put forward the same suggestion, but when it was pointed out to me by the Superintendent of Insurance that the Deputy Minister of Justice, who had argued this case up to and before the Privy Council, was of opinion that those words should not be inserted, I bowed in deference to his opinion.
Will the minister state the reasons for his opinion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know
what reasons the Deputy Minister of Justice had for his opinion, but I am quite satisfied that although the words are not inserted the effect is practically the same as if the words were in. My hon. friend seems to think that the Parliament of Canada or the legislatures of the provinces cannot legislate with respect to foreign corporations.
I did not Say that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I agree that my hon. friend did not say that they could not legislate, but he rather indicated that they did so very rarely-indeed, that it was an improper thing for them to do. But it is a very common thing to do. Take the case of a company incorporated under the laws of Ontario which desires to carry on business in Manitoba. Application is made on its behalf to the legislature of Manitoba and an Act is'passed which makes the company, for the purpose of that Act, a Manitoba incorporation. It proceeds,
4 p.m. therefore, to carry on business in Manitoba under the authority of that legislation; otherwise it could not lawfully carry on business in that province. There is no doubt that this Parliament cannot make an American corporation into a Canadian corporation; that is to say, it cannot give it any wider powers; it cannot cut down its original powers. But it can limit the exercise of those powers within Canada; it can determine the conditions under which that company shall carry on business in Canada, and it may declare that that company ie deemed to be a 'Canadian corporation in the carrying on of the business which if is authorized to carry on. We desire to make if perfectly clear that this Parliament has authority to require a foreign corporation to take out a license and to conform to the provisions of this Act before carrying on business in Canada. That is a point that might be con-

tested. In order to make that absolutely beyond legal question, we enact here that a foreign corporation-I shall quote the language of the section:
Any company other than a Canadian company which may obtain from the minister a license or a renewal of a license shall thereupon and thereby become and be and be deemed to he a company incorporated under the laws . of Canada with power to carry on throughout Canada, or in such part or parts of Canada as may be specified in the license, the various branches or kinds of insurance which the license may authorize.
The purpose of that subsection is perfectly clear to me, and I think it is to my hon. friend. In order to give .the Dominion Government plenary authority over this company in carrying on the business of insurance within Canada, it is to be deemed to be, .and by this legislation becomes, for the purposes of this Act, a company incorporated under the laws of Canada. The *question might be raised before the courts or before the Privy Council as to the constitutionality of this law; as to whether the Dominion Government had the right to require a foreign corporation to take out a license before it could do business in Canada, or make provision as to how it should carry on its business after obtaining the license. A sufficient answer to that would be: by this legislation, within the clear limits of its constitutional authority, the Dominion Parliament declares this foreign corporation to be a Canadian company, with power to carry on business as permitted by the license which it has taken out.
At first blush I had the same view -that my -hon. friend now has, that we-should insert .the words " for the purposes of this Act. ' I used almost the same language as my hon. friend. But when the responsible legal advisor of the Government, who has lived on this case, took an opposite view, and with much greater modesty than is possessed by my .hon. friend from St. John,
I thought his opinion and not mine should govern, and gave way; because we .axe enacting here a measure that has to .stand the test of the law courts, and with .all due deference to. the hon. member for St. John, no matter what respect I may have for him as a legislator-and I shall make no statement on that to-day-I would rather have the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice on a strictly legal point in a case with which he has been identified for so long a period.	*

The extraordinary
nature of this legislation is my excuse for taking up a little more of the time of the

House. The difference between the minister and imys-elf with regard to modesty is that mine is normal and his abnormal; the modesty he has shown to-day is certainly abnormal. Surely when the minister comes to us with a piece of legislation in regard to the terms of which he is surrendering bis own judgment to the judgment of the legal advisor of the Government, he ought to be in a .position to tell us why the legal advisor insists upon this extraordinary language being used, language which did not commend itself to the judgment of the Minister of Finance in the first place. The Minister of Finance has studied law. L would say that he is a good lawyer. He has had a long business training, and I would regard his judgment upon a matter of business legislation as exceedingly good. He comes here to-day and tells us that his judgment has been overruled, and he asks Parliament to adopt this extraordinary piece of legislation-legislation which creates a foreign company, the moment it obtains a license, a corporation under .the laws of 'Canada, not merely for the purposes of this Act, but for all purposes. The foreign company is thus created a Canadian corporation under the laws of Canada, not under this Act merely, but under any law which relates to companies incorporated ini Canada. I think the minister ought to tell us why that change was made. Why would'-it not be sufficient simply to declare that no company other than a Canadian company shall be allowed to do- business in Canada without first obtaining a license therefor f-rom the Minister of Finance, and on obtaining said license such company shall become -subject to the provisions of this Act. That surely would be sufficient. Why it is necessary to -make this radical departure from what is recognized as good legislation, and to declare a foreign company a company incorporated under the laws of Canada, I fail to understand. I do not think the minister believes for a single moment that this is good legislation. I think he realizes that his own view was the correct one. The company might properly be named a corporation for the purposes of this Act. I think that is the minister's own view, and yet he yields to the view of someone else. Whether the deputy minister has personally given his opinion, or whether it was simply some official under him, I do not know, but the minister asks this Parliament, as if we had no sense or intelligence, to pass this extraordinary legislation against what was his own view when he was first considering the Act, and
against what I believe is his own view today. He is not able to give us a single reason why this language should be used.

I do not know anything about the law and I have no right to discuss a legal point, but it looks to me that section 2 simply intends to make these companies Canadian companies in so far as doing business in Canada under this Act is concerned. I do not see that it affects the companies under any other Act. It seems to me the section will accomplish what we are trying to dor

Let us insert the words "for the purpose of this Act." I beg to move that the after the word " Canada " in line 7, the words " for. the purpose of this Act " be inserted. That would avoid the absurdity which would otherwise be in the -statute. It would do no harm, and would clearly carry out what I believe is the intention of th^ committee.

All the big companies
have copies of this Act and they have not complained so far as I know.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think it would be wise to adopt this amendment. It was considered by the Banking and Commerce Committee and the Deputy Minister of Justice advised against it. My hon. friend asks for a reason why it should not be inserted. The onus is on him to show that it should be inserted, but I will give him one reason why it should not be inserted. Its tendency would be to qualify and cut down the effect of the language as it now stands. By this legislation which is thought to be necessary in ordeT to make this Insurance Act constitutional, it is provided that:
Any company other than a Canadian company which may obtain from the minister a license or a renewal of a license shall thereupon and thereby become and be and he deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada with power to carry on throughout Canada, or in such part or parts of Canada as may he specified in the license, the various branches or kinds of insurance which the license may authorize.
That imquestionably brings that foreign company under the jurisdiction of this Parliament. Now if the amendment of my hon. friend were accepted-and I have stated that it had occurred to me that such an amendment might be inserted-the effect would be to diminish the strength of the section as it now stands, by qualifying it. How qualifying it? For the purposes of this Act. I have no doubt in my mind that the effect of the section as it now stands is that

for the purposes of this Act the foreign company becomes a Canadian corporation, but as the matter is so important from a constitutional standpoint, and as the Department of Justice has specially advised against our qualifying it
Was it the deputy minister? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, so I am informed by the Superintendent of Insurance, who took this matter up with him. Therefore I am unwilling to consent to the amendment, although I suggested the same amendment to the Banking and Commerce Committee myself. Our object is to make the provision constitutionally valid beyond all question.
With all due deference to the hon. .member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), a constitutional question is a legal question, and I do not see how members of this House can override the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice and change language which has been considered for the definite purpose of making the constitutionality of the provision beyond question.

I move:
That the words "for the purposes of this Act" be inserted after the word "Canada" in line 7 of subsection 2 of section 4.
How can that injuriously affect the constitutionality of this section? The minister must bear in mind that we are charged with some responsibility, and if we are not going to express our opinion and decide according to our judgment there is no object in consulting this committee, and we might as well remain outside and let the chairman and the minister pass the Bill through without us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I should not like the hon. member for St. John to hold the view that I object to taking his opinion, or to considering the amendment. I am only answering what he said.

If the Minister of Justice, in his place and with the responsibility that rests upon him as a minister, says it is better to leave these words out, I am quite willing to yield to his view, but to ask us to put through a clause absurd and nonsensical upon its face-and I do not hesitate to say it-incorporating a foreign company as a corporation under the general laws of Canada, strikes me as something the minister should not do without having the assurance of the committee that those words will in some way affect the constitu-

tionality of the section, or prevent the carrying out of its purpose.	[DOT]
Why not allow the clause to stand until my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) satisfies himself in regard to the point he raises?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If this is voted upon I shall direct the attention of the Deputy Minister of Justice to the debate which has taken place on this section, and if he sees fit to' change his view, I will bring the matter before the House again at a later stage. I do not like to be put in the position of passing upon the opinion of Deputy Minister of Justice, or having it overridden by the hon. member for St. John. I would rather have it voted upon here, and afterwards if the Deputy Minister of Justice feels that the views of the hon. member for St. John can be met without in any -way weakening the effect of the section, I si all be agreeable to meet his views.

That only shows the
minister is determined to put the section through just as it is, without being able to tell the committee that there is any reason for it, and even going the length of telling the committee that it is against his own judgment, and that it is put through because an official of the department, for whom we all have great respect, thinks it is desirable. The Minister of Justice is the responsible minister of this House, so far as legal questions are concerned. I do not think the Minister of Finance should hesitate to yield to such a reasonable request as I have made. I can assure him that by doing so he will not lose any time in the consideration of the measure. I do not wish to overrule the view of the Deputy Minister of Justice; possibly he is right and I am wrong. I have often been wrong, but sometimes I am right. It is just possible I may have hit upon the right interpretation of this section. I am constrained to-believe the Deputy Minister of Justice is wrong in the view he has taken. This is a very important matter. We are establishing a precedent in legislation, when we declare that foreign companies shall become companies incorporated under the laws of' Canada. We are establishing for all time,, precedents, which I do not believe exist in any other country in the civilized world. That being so, we should not hesitate for a moment to take the advice and guidances of the Minister of Justice.
Amendment negatived on division.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I stated to the House that this question was raised by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and an amendment suggested substantially in the terms of the amendment made by my hon. friend from St. John. That amendment was submitted to the Deputy Minister of Justice, who stated it was unnecessary and objectionable. The reason I have asked that my hon. friend's amendment should be voted down is because he seemed to impugn my word with respect to what had been done. I will say to my hon. friend, because I am just as anxious-
If my hon. friend will permit me, I did not impugn his word at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was the effect of what my hon. friend said. He said we should get the opinion of the Department of Justice. As a matter of fact, we have the opinion of the Department of Justice. The Deputy Minister of Justice has been connected with this insurance case from the beginning to the end. I will submit the amendment to him, and if in his opinion it can be adopted, without weakening the effect of the section, I will see it is included.
Let me say again to my hon. friend that I did not impugn his word at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not in so many words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have to insert after the word " or," in the 16th line, the words " any association of persons." The reason is to more accurately describe the
system of inter-insurance, which is not. confined to individuals, but applies to corporations as well. The use of the word " persons " would cover both cases.
Is this a new section?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is practically the same as in the old Act.

I see that it authorizes a number of individuals to be licensed to carry on insurance business. Is there any limit to the subjects that this association would insure? In Lloyds you can take out a wager policy. You can get a policy, for example, that the war will terminate before the end of the present year by paying a sufficient premium. Perhaps you could get a policy that the present Government would win the next election, ibut in that case it would require an enormous rate of premium. Does this mean that when an association is licensed to do business it can do *any kind of business it wishes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; it can only do the business it is authorized to do under the license. We have authority to license a company to carry on the class of wagering business referred to by my hon. friend, but in .the exercise of our discretion I think it probable we would not do it. There is power to do it. They might apply for such a license and we -would have to consider the question whether we should issue it or not. So far we have not granted licenses for so-called freak insurance.
The license itself will indicate the kind of business that is permitted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Why is the word "individuals " used in reference to the word " association " on line 3, and in the amendment you use the word "persons?" Is there a different interpretation for the word. " persons " from that of the word " individuals?" " Persons " would include a corporation, while " individuals " would not. Is it intended in one case to exclude corporations and in the other to admit them?

The word "individuals " -would not include " corporations," but it is the correct word to use in. respect ito Lloyds, because Lloyds is not a. corporation, but an association of .individuals. I think there is no question, about the propriety of this definition of Lloyds. Now we come down to .the amendment " or to any association of persons." That word.

" persons " is wide enough, to embrace corporations as well ias individuals.
Subsection as amended agreed to.
On section 4, subsection 4-provincial companies:

What is meant by
"faculty?"

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed
by the superintendent that the word "faculty" is used by the Privy Council in its judgment. It is not a usual word, but the idea is to make this legislation constitutional having regard to that decision.

This is a very important section. If it passes in its present form the effect will be that a company incorporated and under the control of a pro-vinieal legislature upon obtaining a license from the Minister of Finance becomes a company incorporated undeT the laws of Canada. Therefore, it would, ipso facto, 'be in the future entirely amenable to the laws of Parliament and would be taken wholly out of the jurisdiction of the provincial legislature which gave it life.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is the same question we were discussing a few moments ago.

It is a little broader
here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The judgement of the Privy Council was to the effect that the Dominion Parliament has no jurisdiction over a provinoially incorporated insurance company which not only does business in its own province but outside of that province. In other words, a provincially incorporated insurance company, no matter whether confining its business to the province of its incorporation or carrying on business under proper legislative authority in other provinces of Canada, is not within the jurisdiction of the Dominion Parliament unless it submits itself to such jurisdiction. The effect of this subsection is to permit provincially incorporated companies to submit themselves to Dominion jurisdiction, as many of them will. It is necessary that we should make them Dominion companies so as to have jurisdiction over them once they take out a license, and it is necessary in the opinion of the Deputy Minister of Justice that we should make a provincial corporation a Canadian company so as to give us jurisdiction over it.

Could that not be worked out in some way without removing them

*wholly from the jurisdiction of the .provincial legislature?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think we have wholly removed them.

It says:
4. The minister may grant to a provincial company which has the faculty or capacity to carry on its business throughout Canada and to obtain the license hereinafter mentioned, and has complied with the provisions of this Act in that behalf applicable to a Canadian company, a license authorizing the company to carry bn its said business or any part thereof throughout Canada or in any part or parts of Canada comprising more than one province which may be specified in the license, and the company shall thereupon and thereby become and he and he deemed to he a company incorporated under the laws of Canada.
I venture to say that the moment that license is taken out, although that is the object of it, the effect will be to remove these provincial companies, incorporated by the provincial legislatures, having certain restrictions which the legislatures have thought wise to impose upon them, ipso facto from the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures. They will become Dominion corporations incorporated under the laws of Canada, which means this Parliament, and it seems to me they then become subject only to the jurisdiction of this Parliament. Have the governments of the different provinces been communicated with about this clause?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Bill has been sent to all the provincial departments of insurance many weeks ago. I do not agree that these provincial companies become by this legislation Dominion companies in the sense that my hon. friend has in mind. I do not believe their charters are repealed or that this Government has authority to repeal their charters. Their capitalization and powers', and any statutory provisions applicable to them as provincial incorporations, all remain in full force and effect. If a company obtains a license and wants to oarry on business in Canada under that license, then it becomes a Dominion company subject -to this Act. My hon. friend knows' as a lawyer that very nice constitutional questions may arise. It is said that there is no legislation through which you cannot drive a coach and four. It may be that they will try to drive one through this, but this is the language which has been recommended by the Justice Department and by special counsel to meet the situation created by the Privy Council's decision.

For example, take a
company incorporated in Nova Scotia, with a provision in its Act of incorporation that the head office of the company shall be 'in Nova Scotia. By section 51 the shareholders may change the head office from one province to another. If they should move the head office from Halifax to Toronto, which Act will govern, the Act under which the company was incorporated in Nova Scotia or this Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that what the public should do in this case is to call in a lawyer and take his advice. That is a hard one.
Mr. PiUGSLEY: That is going to be the effect of this Act, if it is not the intention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
will realize that we are confronted with a condition and not a theory. The condition is that the Privy 'Council has said that the Dominion Parliament has no jurisdiction to regulate the business of an insurance company incorporated by a provincial legislature carrying on business, in its own province, or even outside its province. If we had this Act, many provincially incorporated insurance companies would desire, for the sake of their standing if nothing else, to be subject to Dominion jurisdiction. One way in which they could bring themselves within the Dominion jurisdiction, although difficulties might arise, would be to take out Dominion incorporation and have the assets and liabilities of the old company assigned* to the new. This provision has been inserted to give such companies the right to make application to take out an insurance license and subject themselves to the jurisdiction of the Dominion Insurance Act. It is pointed out to me by the Superintendent of Insurance that this provision has been in the Act for many years, that the principle of licensing provincial companies is not a new one, but one of many years' standing.
These words axe entire ly new.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Some of them.
Are not the words " and the company shall thereupon and 'thereby become and be deemed to be a company incorporated under the laws of Canada " entirely new?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
And they are the vital words of the section of which I am complaining.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
They are the
vital words, and the words intended to give the Dominion jurisdiction.
And to take the jurisdiction out of the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For the purposes of this Act.

Why not say so. I urge that after the word " Canada " in line 18, the words " for the purposes of this Act " should he inserted. If you do not do that you are sure to have litigation. The minister speaks of getting rid of litigation. But he is opening a wide door, and for years in the future the lawyers will rise up and call him blessed and say what a great man he has been for the profession, and how many trips he has given them across to the Privy Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, they are
a good lot.

Yes, they are good fellows. How is it possible to argue that this is not going to take jurisdiction out of the provincial legislatures? Here is a provincial company which comes and gets a license. There would be no objection to declaring that it is to become, for the purposes of this Aot, subject to the jurisdiction of the Department of Finance and is not to be permitted to carry on business except under the terms of this license. That would be quite reasonable and possible, but for some occult reason hidden in the minds of the officers of the Justice Department that has not yet penetrated the mind of the Minister of Finance, this Parliament is declaring that the moment the company obtains its license it, ipso facto, becomes what it is not, and what nobody can pretend it is- in the words of the Act it " shall thereupon and thereby become and be deemed to be a company incorporated 'under the laws of Canada." I have asked the minister to put in the words " for the purpose of this Act." It appears he will not do it, because, for some mysterious reason, it may impair the validity of the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will say the same thing as I said before: if the sense of the House is that these words should be inserted, or if the Minister of Justice, after looking into the matter, is of the opinion that these words may be inserted without weakening the effqct of the section, I will see that they are inserted.
Stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I want it carried.
It strikes the minister's pride. He wants it carried.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I told the hon. gentleman from St. John that this amendment had been inserted at my request in the Banking and Commerce Committee. I told him that after the words had been inserted, the deputy minister advised that they should be left out, and they were left out. It seems to me the onus, so to speak, is not upon me to insert those words, and then have them taken out afterwards, but I think we should pass the section as it stands, on the understanding that I will again consult the Minister of Justice, and draw his attention to the observations of the hon. gentleman from St. John, and, if necessary, the section can be amended at a later stage.

July 16, 1917.
Sir,-I have the honour to reply to your letter of oth instant submitting a draft Bill respecting the Toronto, Hamilton & Buffalo Railway Company, with a request for my opinion upon the question whether Parliament has power to amend or vary the agreement exhibited in the schedule to the Bill.
The parties to this agreement, which is dated November 15, 1897, are the Hamilton & Dun-das Street Railway Company, a provincial company incorporated under a special Act of the Legislature of Ontario, Statutes of 1876, chapter 87, and the Toronto, Hamilton & Buffalo Railway Company, which, though originally incorporated by a special Act of the Legislature of Ontario, Statutes of 1847, chapter 75, became a Dominion corporation under chapter 86, Statutes of Canada, 1891, which declared its undertaking to be a work for the general advantage of Canada, and the company to be a company subject to the jurisdiction of Parliament.
By clause 8 of the agreement it is provided that the contract shall continue in force for the period of twenty-one years, and for a further period of twenty-nine years if the sane-

tion of Parliament and the Legislature be obtained to legalize this extension. This provision, ex facie, suggests that neither of the contracting corporations had the capacity or power to bind itself by such an agreement for a period exceeding twenty-one years, and the railway legislation in force at the time the agreement was entered into (Revised Statutes of Ontario, 1S97, chapter 207, section 77, and Statutes of Canada, 1888, chapter 29, section 238) indicates this to be the fact. The Legislature of Ontario, on the petition of the Hamilton & Dundas Street Railway Company and the town of Dundas, appears to have ratified the agreement by chapter 60, Statutes of Ontario, 1898, and now Parliament is asked to do likewise on behalf of the Toronto, Hamilton & Buffalo Railway Company.
I observe that upon representations made on behalf of the town of Dundas, the railway Committee of the House of Commons has recommended an amendment to the Bill which will have the effect of extending the agreement merely for four years, i.e., until 1922, instead of the period of twenty-nine years contemplated by the agreement; that the authority of Parliament to make such an alteration in the terms of the agreement has been questioned in the House, and that it is under these circumstances that the matter is referred.
The proposed amendment to the Bill obviously would effect a material change in the terms of the original agreement, and in my opinion this is incompetent to Parliament, seeing that the Hamilton & Dundas Street Railway company is a provincial corporation and consequently that its contract rights and obligations are not within the legislative authority of Parliament.
I have the honour to be, Sir,

As to dredging, the present condition at Margaree Harbour, is the result, in part, of xthe destruction of the piers which protect the channel from the sand flow. I wish the minister would rush the dredge there as rapidly as possible, as no company will undertake this work after September 15. The work should really have been done in June or July. The minister was good enough to promise me early this season- that this work would be undertaken with as little delay as possible. Needless to say, I am disappointed.

We have already called for tenders for this work. I will see about the tenders at once, and see that the work is gone on with.

About 20 years ago this Government adopted the policy in a number of cases of assisting the provincial governments in the construction of wharves. In more recent years still there has been a special vote for the building of these wharves. These have all been omitted from the present estimates. Upon the St. John river and other non-tidal waters in New Brunswick, there are a number of wharves in need of repairs and these repairs have been made from the vote to which I refer.

With respect to the breakwater at Negro Point, we called for tenders some two or three years ago, but the tender price at that time seemed very high. I think it was something like $600,-DOO or $700,000; but the work they proposed was to be carried out by the use of granite instead of the ordinary stone, and a further plan has been prepared for the use of stone from Partridge Island, and we expect to be able to get the work done much cheaper by the use of. granite. We are going to call for tenders in a few days. This work is absolutely necessary to protect the harbour on the west side of St. John, and I am going to propose, before Parliament closes, that we vote an amount sufficient to carry out the work of building the breakwater, on the recommendation of the engineers that it is necessary to preserve the berths that have already been constructed in the west harbour of St. John.
Mr. PUiGSLEY: I suppose those estimates will be ready in a few days?

With regard to the depth of the water at the berths, I noticed in the papers-, either to-day or yesterday, that the United States authorities have been informed that if they would dredge out Portland harbour to a depth of 35 feet for the larger vessels, the Canadian Government, during the war at all events, would be very glad to avail themselves of Portland harbour in connection with the Canadian export trade. That is a matter in regard to which the people of the Maritime Provinces are naturally very jealous. After a long struggle, commencing thirty years ago, the people of the Maritime Provinces succeeded in getting St. John and Halifax recognized as the winter ports of Canada. I should be very sorry indeed to see any change in the policy in that regard. Of course the ques-fMr. Rogers ]	.
tion which is raised as to deepening the harbour of Portland to 35 feet is an important one, if that depth is required for the safety of the largest vessels which come to Atlantic ports, and if St. John harbour is not deepened. Is it proposed to make the depth of water at the berths in St. John harbour 35 feet at low water?

The dredging of the harbour of Portland is, of course, entirely in the hands of the United States Government. I had no knowledge that there was any proposal to adopt Portland harbour as against the harbours of St. John or Halifax. No Canadian who has a knowledge of our harbours and of the amount that has been expended in their improvement and development would think of doing anything to disturb our programme of developing our own harbours and carrying our traffic through our own ports. That is the policy of the Government; everything will be done to develop the harbour of St. John, where a great increase of trade has taken place during the last couple of years. That policy, so far as I am aware, will be continued in the future, in order that we may develop these harbours as rapidly as possible to keep pace with the increasing trade.

In the very interesting statement which he has made-a statement which, I am sure, will be appreciated by the people of St, John, my hon. friend has omitted to answer my question whether it is proposed to have a depth of 35 feet at low water so as to afford sufficient accommodation for the larger ships. My hon. friend says that he has not seen any suggestion with regard to the use of Portland harbour for Canadian trade. If he will look at to-morrow morning's papers he will see that a very interesting situation has arisen in Congress in consequence of a letter which the British Ambassador wrote a few days ago to a member of the United States Senate approving of the proposed deepening of Portland harbour in order to accommodate Canadian export trade. A question has been raised in Congress as to the interference with the internal affairs of the United States by the ambassador of a foreign Government. Some senators have suggested that the British Ambassador ought not to express any opinion whatever as to the expenditure of any money in Portland harbour. In his letter, the British Ambassador -he is authorized by the Canadian Government to say so-says that if the harbour is deepened to 35 feet, the Canadian Government will use it for a large part of its

trade during the winter. It would be unfortunate if the Government by reason of stopping short of the depth which is necessary for the accommodation of the largest ocean vessels, should lose the trade which legitimately belongs to Canadian ports. I trust that my hon. friend will take that into his careful consideration in connection with the deepening of the present berths and also with regard to any new berths that may be constructed.

We are dredging to a
depth of 32 feet at low tide at St. John. I did not know that there was any necessity for going deeper. Of course, if it is necessary to go deeper, we will have to make provision for it and dredge the other three feet. It has not been brought prominently to the notice of the department that the depth of 35 feet was necessary. As to the statement of the British Ambassador, I confess that I had not heard of it. I am glad, however, to be able to inform my hon. friend that the British Ambassador has not interfered with our programme of deepening and developing the harbour of St. John. My hon. friend can rest assured that all our energies will be bent to the development of our own harbours and to preventing the trade of out country from being diverted to any other than our own ports. When I was in England it was suggested that in the case of rush orders it might be more convenient that some of the trade of this country should be shipped through other ports than St. John and Halifax, especially in the winter months. I at once registered a strong objection to any such proposal, and I have not heard of it since. I believe the course that I adopted on that occasion had the effect of changing the minds of those who had that course in view. That is the only time that I ever heard any such proposal. As I have said, the country can depend upon it that the Government will do everything in their power to develop as rapidly as possible our own harbours in order that they may 'be able to take care of all Canadian trade.

The minister states that the matter of going below 32 feet had not been brought to his notice. I regret to leam that, because in 1911 when I was minister I determined upon sinking the crib sites to a depth of 40 feet. The object of that was to allow for the depth of water in the berths being 35 feet, my idea being that the crib sites should be at least five feet below the level of the berths. I did that because I was aware that the
246J
harbour of New York is dredged to a depth of either 40 or 45 feet-to 40 feet at least. Ships are getting bigger every year, and there are a large number of ships crossing the Atlantic to-day which would not come into a harbour where there was not 32 feet of water at the berths; it would not be safe for them to come, they want 35 feet to avoid the danger of the ship scraping along the bottom. There is always more or less filling in from the surrounding water; that is going on all the time at St. John harbour. S(f I concluded six years ago that in order to bring St. John harbour up to first-class standing it was necessary to provide in the very near future for a berth of 35 feet, and that is why I made provision for sinking the crib sites to a depth of 40 feet. I would like very much if the minister would consider making provision for a depth of 35 feet at the new berths. The very fact that the British Ambassador has put himself in writing in reference to the proposed deepening of the Portland harbour to a depth of 35 feet, stating that if that were done the Canadian Government would use that harbour for purposes of transport during the war, shows that the big shipping companies -demand that depth of water for the safety of their large vessels. It is all' very well to have an open harbour like St. John; it is all very well to have a large number of berths, which we are striving for, but unless we have them to the proper depth the big ships will not come, and our Maritime Province harbours will not be regarded as first class harbours to which the most important trade of the world can come. In my judgment-and I am speaking from information received from those most qualified to speak on the subject-we shall not be able to attract to our harbours the big ships trading on the Atlantic unless we have a depth of at least 35 feet at the berths.

There may be some force in what my hon. friend has said, but it is hardly likely that within the next few years there will be any larger ships on the Atlantic than there are to-day. It is probable that the ships will he smaller and more numerous. My hon. friend's remarks remind me that a couple of years ago, when we were considering the construction of a dry dock at Esquimalt and Halifax, the Admiralty stoutly stuck to their request that we have a depth of something like 40 feet. So I am inclined to think there may be some force in what my hon. friend has said, and the department will give his sug-

gestion careful consideration, and see whether it is necessary to have a depth of 35 feet of water at berths 16 and 17 at St. J ohn.

May I impose on the good nature of the minister for a few moments io draw his attention to the unfortunate position in which the town of Sackville is placed through lack of wharf accommodation. A few years ago when
10	p.m. my hon. friend from St.
John (Mr. Pugsley) was Minister of Public Works, we impressed upon him the necessity of giving us very much improved wharf accommodation, with the result that an appropriation was made and a contract let for a new wharf a little removed from the old location. This wharf, which cost something like $40,000, was partly completed when the present Minister of Public Works took office, and has been finally completed since. We had hoped, of course, that when- the new wharf was completed the railway would run a spur dowij to it, which would give the people of Sackville proper wharf facilities. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane), however, for some reason or another,-if anybody in that locality advised him to act as he did, it was bad advice-refused to build the spur, and the people in that portion of the county of Westmorland are now in the unfortunate position of having no wharf accommodation at all. Those who do not know the Minister of Railways as well as I do, might think that this had been done purposely, but I would not for a moment charge the minister with discrimination against the people of Sackville. At all events the spur line was not constructed. Since then the Minister of Public Works has made a reasonably large expenditure for repairing the old wharf, where we had rail connection. I do not know the exact cost of that work, but the wharf was repaired, and while the accommodation was not sufficient it was better than none at all. Last spring, however, the Minister of Railways, apparently learning that the people of Sackville were getting some accommodation, tore up the rails from the old wharf and we are now absolutely without any rail connection to the public wharf at all. I am just in receipt of a letter today from Sackville which says that the ice has carried some portion of the old bed away, and a vessel which arrived there within the past week to discharge a cargo put out to sea again without discharging her cargo, because at that point there is a tidal river and when the tide dropped the

vessel slid because of the condition of the bed. I think the minister should see to it that immediate attention is paid to the river bed near the wharf so that vessels may discharge their cargo in safety. It would need only a small appropriation, and could be made under the general heading of improvements to harbours and rivers, I suppose. It would hardly be necessary for the minister to send the engineer down there, because the caretaker of the wharf would be able to have the bed of the wharf attended to so that vessels could discharge their cargo. I think the new wharf was completed in 1912, at an expenditure of $40,000. I do not believe a vessel has ever tied up to it yet, and it would seem to me that unless the minister puts some one in charge of the wharf it will be falling into disrepair. I would therefore urge him to have his engineer in that section of the country keep his eye on the wharf, because I still have hopes that we may get rail communication with it yet.
I hope when that is done we shall have our new wharf in a proper -state of repair, and will be able to use it. I only -make the latter reference and suggestion in the interest of the department, because after that amount of money has been spent there the wharf should not be allowed to go into decay, or to get out of repair, for the sake of the small expenditure necessary to keep it in good condition.

My hon. friend will quite appreciate the fact that I am not very well acquainted with -the local conditions of the two wharves he deals with, but I shall be very glad -to have the matter looked into by the engineers and see if anything can be done tending to an improvement.

If there is an urgent

What is the nature of the work at Laprairie?
Building a roadway.

Last spring I went across Victoria bridge and I found four or five feet of water on that road. In the early spring we find about fifty feet of ice on the road and it stops traffic there for six or seven days. It is the only way of reaching Montreal from the south side of the St. Lawrence. Is it the intention to spend this money during next summer?

We have had a good deal of trouble with this particular work. The work acts as a dyke and a protection and also as a road. A contract was recently let for its completion and the contractors are at work. They have promised to have 100 or 200 men at work every day from Monday next in order that they may get it completed as soon as possible.
Who are the contractors?
The Carleton Construction Company.

Seventy-nine thousand
dollars.

The minister expects
the work will soon be through?
We want to try and get it through this fall.

It is an eyesore. People travelling out of Montreal are stopped immediately at the outlet of the city. I have been over that route on several occasions. If the minister completes that work at the earliest possible date he will render great service to the travelling public.

Last year we built a temporary length of road which gave good service for a time. We are pressing the contractors and urging them to get the work completed as rapidly as possible.
